Case Information: An 88-year-old female was found lying down. Upon admission, she exhibited nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, and a slow heart rate. Her medical history includes essential hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypothyroidism, chronic renal failure (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes G3a classification), ischemic stroke, and osteoporosis. Her medications included insulin (12 IU daily), levothyroxine (100 µg daily), losartan (50 mg twice daily), metoprolol (50 mg daily), amiodarone (200 mg daily), simvastatin (40 mg daily), metformin (500 mg twice daily), and omeprazole (20 mg daily). Initial vital signs showed a temperature of 35.6°C, blood pressure of 90/44 mmHg with a mean arterial pressure of 59 mmHg, heart rate of 45 beats per minute, oxygen saturation of 92% requiring supplementary nasal oxygen, and a regular respiratory rate. Physical examination revealed dehydrated skin, pupils equal in size and reactive to light, and confusion (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14) without focal neurological deficits. Her extremities were cold, with livedo reticularis (Mottling score of 3), and no edema.
Diagnostic Tests: The initial electrocardiogram (EKG) demonstrated the presence of sinus bradycardia. Subsequently, a junctional pattern developed, accompanied by peaked T waves, mainly from V2 to V4, depression of the ST segment from V4 to V6, and diffuse nonspecific ST-segment abnormalities. QRS prolongation and ST shortening were not present. Blood tests revealed hyperlactatemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction, and microcytic anemia. Myocardial injury was investigated with troponin levels which showed no elevation (14.4 pg/mL; 17.2 pg/mL). Point-of-care ultrasound revealed a bilateral A-line pattern with lung sliding, cardiac output was estimated at 1.6 L/minute, and the collapsibility index of the inferior vena cava was 24%. Urgent echocardiography was performed in the ICU and was compatible with normal biventricular systolic function with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 75% during dobutamine administration.

Case Information: A 27-year-old male patient presented for refractive surgery with no reported medical or ocular history. His manifest refraction was −3.00 −1.50 × 90 in the right eye and −4.75 DS in the left eye, with a corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA) of 20/15 in both eyes. Examination revealed a 2.5 mm × 3 mm paracentral nummular scar in the corneal stroma at the 2 o'clock position in the right eye. After obtaining informed consent, an uneventful LASIK procedure was performed using the AMO IntraLase femtosecond laser. Flap diameters were 8.4 mm in the right eye and 8.3 mm in the left eye, with a thickness of 100 μm. The optical zone was 6.5 mm with a transitional zone of 1.25 mm in both eyes, using the WaveLight EX500 Excimer Laser. Postoperative treatment included ofloxacin 0.3% four times daily for one week, ketorolac 0.5% drops twice daily for 3 days, prednisolone acetate 1% drops four times daily for 1 month followed by a slow taper of fluorometholone 0.1% drops, and artificial tears. The first 3 months post-surgery were unremarkable, with manifest refraction of +0.25 −0.25 × 101 in the right eye and +0.50 −0.50 × 41 in the left eye, and uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) of 20/20 in both eyes. Ten months post-surgery, the patient reported blurry vision in the right eye for several days, with UDVA declining to 20/50 in the right eye.
Diagnostic Tests: Slit-lamp examination revealed fine KPs and diffuse corneal edema. Specular microscopy imaging of the right eye endothelium was unsuccessful and failed to show good endothelial integrity compared to the left eye.

Case Information: A 21-year-old male visited the orthopedic outpatient department with a history of left hip pain persisting for 1 year after a minor fall. The patient reported difficulty in performing heavy strenuous activities such as running, jumping, and other sports activities. Pain was noted at the terminal range of movements. The FABER test yielded a positive result. The patient was able to actively raise his leg.
Diagnostic Tests: Radiograph left hip revealed a radiolucent swelling along inferior part of neck with a well-defined, eccentric osteolytic lesion involving subcapital region of the left femoral neck. The lesion was oval shaped and without any calcification or periosteal reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) suggested of cystic lesion involving synovial lining near head-and-neck junction of the left femur. Histopathological examination showed lobular pattern with stellate to spindle-shaped cells on the myxoid background. Few osteoclast type of giant cells were found in the periphery of the lobules. Tumor cells had oval- to spindle-shaped nucleus with surrounding densely eosinophilic cytoplasm within a myxoid background.

Case Information: A 13-year-old male student presented with a flattening of the right anterior chest wall since birth. He had no symptoms other than cosmetic concerns. He was the second child in his family, with no similar presentations or associated familial disorders reported. Physical examination showed normal growth parameters and IQ. There were no abnormal craniofacial findings. The chest wall was asymmetric with underdevelopment on the right side. The patient exhibited normal strength in the right upper limb and a full range of motion in the shoulder joint. Both limbs were symmetric with no finger anomalies. Auscultation of the chest revealed normal heart sounds, breath sounds, and respiration pattern.
Diagnostic Tests: Computed tomography scan revealed that the pectoralis major muscle was underdeveloped, but the pectoralis minor muscle and the anterior serratus muscle were present. Radiological examination of the chest showed no abnormalities of the ribs or heart.

Case Information: A 1-month-old male infant was brought in with a swelling located in the occipital region, which had been present since birth. The parents reported that the swelling had gradually increased in size to its current dimensions of 14 cm × 12 cm. The affected area featured dysplastic skin and was encircled by a ring of coarse hair. The lesion had a cystic appearance and contained clear fluid. It was compressible, nonpulsatile, transilluminant, and its size and tension remained unchanged regardless of the infant's position or crying.
Diagnostic Tests: Computed tomography scan of the head revealed a 14 cm subcutaneous mass of soft tissue density similar to the brain tissue, with no intracranial communication. The brain parenchyma appeared unremarkable.

Case Information: A 25-year-old male came for an eye examination due to a gradual decrease in visual acuity in his left eye over the past few years. The patient and his family noted that he had difficulty fixating with the left eye since early childhood. He sought medical attention hoping for improvement. There was no history of trauma, ocular surgery, or any other interventions. The family confirmed that his vision had been poor since childhood. On physical examination, the patient exhibited distinctive facial and body features. There were areas of hypopigmented hair on both forearms. Facial features included synophrys, a high nasal root, a prominent nasal root, and a white forelock of hair. Oral examination revealed a high-arched palate with dental anomalies such as microdontia, oligodontia, and conical teeth. The patient had no hearing deficits, and there was no relevant family history. Examination also showed lateral displacement of the inner canthi (dystopia canthorum). Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was measured at 21 mm Hg in the right eye and 41 mm Hg in the left eye. Pupil examination was normal in the right eye, while the left eye had a small constricted pupil.
Diagnostic Tests: Slit lamp examination of the right eye showed normal conjunctiva, sclera, and anterior chamber depth with segmental heterochromia and clear crystalline lens. Slit lamp examination of the left eye showed clear cornea, deep and quiet anterior chamber with complete iris hypochromia, a small area of iris transillumination defect and mature cataract. Gonioscopy showed an open angle without peripheral anterior synechiae and with normal angle pigmentation of the left eye. B scan of the left eye showed RD.

Case Information: A 47-year-old female visited for a routine dental checkup. Since birth, she had multiple discrete purple discolorations on the right side of her chin, neck, and lower limb. She reported experiencing blurred vision for the past year. General examination showed stable vital signs. Extraoral examination revealed facial asymmetry on the right side due to soft tissue hypertrophy, with numerous discrete purple lesions on the right frontal region of the face, eyelid, around the nose, chin, and lips. These lesions extended to the back of the neck and shoulder, not crossing the midline. Intraoral examination showed asymptomatic bright-red flat areas of discoloration present from birth on the right postero-lateral border of the hard palate, extending laterally 1.5 cm from the palatal aspect of the free or marginal gingiva near the 17 tooth region, medially 2 cm from the mid-palatine raphe region, posteriorly to the right posterolateral junction of the hard and soft palate, and on the right ventral surface of the floor of the mouth near the lingual aspect of the 44, 45, and 46 tooth regions. The right lateral border of the tongue was also bright red and enlarged. Similar purplish lesions were observed on the flexor and extensor aspects of the right lower limb. The skin lesions were flat, non-elevated, and purplish in color, while the oral lesions were bright red due to the presence of oxygenated blood in fine capillaries.
Diagnostic Tests: Fundoscopic examination of the right eye revealed 'bean-pot cupping' or 'bayoneting' of retinal vessels.

Case Information: A seven-month-old male presented with an eye turn since birth. Examination revealed esotropia at near measuring 60 prism-diopters, alternate fixation with a preference for the right eye, and -4 abduction in both eyes. Cycloplegic refraction was +1.50 diopters in both eyes, and the rest of the ophthalmic examination was unremarkable. Surgical intervention included a 6mm medial rectus muscle recession in both eyes and a 6mm lateral rectus resection in the left eye. One week after surgery, the patient exhibited orthotropia with a palpebral fissure in the left eye that was 1 mm narrower than that of the right eye.
Diagnostic Tests: Forced duction test revealed no resistance to abduction and slight resistance to adduction in either eye.

Case Information: A 42-year-old Caucasian woman, employed as a nurse, presented with an elevated alanine transaminase concentration of 469 U/L (normal range: 10-35) during an evaluation for sub-fertility. Other liver function tests, including albumin levels and coagulation screen, were within normal limits. She exhibited no symptoms or signs indicative of liver disease. Her medical history included recurrent urinary tract infections and previous miscarriages. She was taking folic acid and nitrofurantoin 50 mg daily for the past two years. There was no reported history of excessive alcohol consumption or use of herbal remedies or supplements. Physical examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Additional tests showed a significantly abnormal autoimmune profile, with positive anti-nuclear antibodies at a titre of 1:640, smooth muscle antibodies at a titre of 1:320, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies at a titre of 1:320. Anti-Rho, extractable nuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor were also positive. Immunoglobulin G levels were elevated at 22.8 g/L, while IgA and IgM levels were within normal ranges. Tests for chronic hepatitis viruses were negative, and serum ferritin was measured at 300 μg/L.
Diagnostic Tests: Liver biopsy showed marked chronic inflammation within the portal tracts and extensive fibrosis and some features of cirrhosis.

Case Information: A 10-day-old, full-term Caucasian male infant was admitted to a local hospital with symptoms of viral gastroenteritis. During the hospital stay, pediatric surgical services were consulted due to left scrotal swelling, and a left hydrocele was identified. The patient was subsequently discharged. Seventeen days later, at four weeks of age, the infant returned with a 24-hour history of left scrotal swelling, redness, fever, and a pus-like discharge from an ulcerated area in the left hemi-scrotum. An abdominal examination showed normal results, while a scrotal examination revealed a left scrotal abscess and a hard, swollen left testis. No hernia was detected. Immediate surgical exploration was planned. Intravenous antibiotics (amoxicillin with clavulanic acid and flucloxacillin) and fluids were administered due to the local scrotal infection. A midline raphe scrotal incision was performed, and a small amount of pus was drained. Necrotic scrotal wall tissue was excised back to healthy tissue margins. The tunica vaginalis was noted to be thickened, and the testis was found to be edematous with a normal blood supply. No evidence of testicular torsion was observed. The wound was thoroughly washed with antiseptic solution, and the dartos muscle and skin were closed using absorbable sutures. The fever subsided shortly after surgery, and the swelling, redness, and pain decreased over the next 48 hours.
Diagnostic Tests: Wound cultures revealed Enterococcus sp. (ampicillin-sensitive) and Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-sensitive). Histology confirmed the intra-operative diagnosis.

Case Information: A 52-year-old African American man presented with a history of subcutaneous nodules appearing across various parts of his body and a noticeable reduction in subcutaneous fat. These symptoms emerged twelve years after an initial episode at the age of 34, during which similar nodules were observed but resolved without intervention.
Diagnostic Tests: Skin punch biopsies were taken from the right chest and right forearm, showing lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate primarily involving the subcutis with some extension into the deep dermis and periadnexal fat with abundant mucin deposition. Lymphocytes were CD3+ and CD5+ with a subpopulation of CD8+ and CD4+ T-cells. Staining was positive for beta F1 and most of the CD8+ cells were expressing TIA-1. Stainings for CD30, CD25, and TCR gamma were negative. Laboratory studies showed bi-lineage cytopenias, as well as abnormal liver function tests, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, hypoalbuminemia, and an elevated D-dimer. Serum inflammatory markers were elevated. Positron emission tomography and computerized tomography scans showed nonspecific metabolically active enlarged axillary and inguinal nodes and a normal sized spleen (12.7 cm). Bilateral bone marrow biopsies revealed a hypercellular bone marrow (∼90%) with an atypical polymorphous lymphohistiocytic infiltrate admixed with eosinophils and plasma cells, scattered hemophagocytosis, and no evidence of lymphoma involvement.

Case Information: A 6-year-old female presented with a four-week history of headache and vomiting. The headache was gradual in onset, dull in nature, primarily on the left side, and more severe in the morning, with vomiting providing relief. Additionally, she experienced difficulty with walking. Neurological examination revealed a fully conscious child with normal higher cerebral functions. She exhibited truncal ataxia, but other cerebellar functions were intact. Examination of other systems showed no abnormalities.
Diagnostic Tests: Cranial computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging revealed left cerebellar tumor with obstructive hydrocephalus.

Case Information: A 10-year-old girl was brought to the hospital due to issues with her visual field. She had been experiencing worsening headaches, nausea, and weight loss over the past six months. Her medical history and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, she was initially thought to have gastroenteritis. However, she later developed abducens nerve palsy in her left eye along with visual field disturbances.
Diagnostic Tests: Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the head found a solitary mass with heterogeneous high density in the suprasellar region. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a lobulated mass with a well-defined margin with mixed high-intensity and isointense signal on T1-weighted imaging and mixed low-intensity and high-intensity signal on T2-weighted imaging. These imaging findings suggested the presence of large hemorrhage, necrosis, and small cyst in the tumor. The tumor showed a heterogeneous high-intensity area on diffusion-weighted images, low-intensity area on ADC map. On contrast-enhanced MRI, the tumor exhibited a ring-like enhancement. Microscopic examination revealed that the resected tumor tissue was composed of mononucleated cytotrophoblastic cells and large multinucleated syncytiotrophoblastic cells. Hemorrhage and necrosis were also confirmed. Immunohistochemical staining for hCG was strongly positive.

Case Information: A 54-year-old Japanese woman presented to the outpatient clinic with a 20-year history of subcutaneous fat loss on her left upper limb. She has been receiving treatment for hypothyroidism for 22 years and for chronic rheumatoid arthritis for 11 years. There is no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination at the initial visit showed multifocal subcutaneous fat loss on both upper limbs, shoulders, back, abdomen, and the left lower limb.
Diagnostic Tests: A biopsy specimen from the right shoulder revealed a decrease in adipose tissue, a prominent increase in collagen fibers and dense infiltration of lymphocytes around the vesicles.

Case Information: The patient is a 5-year-old girl from Bihar, India, born to nonconsanguineous parents with a normal perinatal period. She remained healthy until 40 months of age when she experienced acute onset lethargy and confusion following an upper respiratory tract infection, which resolved spontaneously over 5 days. During recovery, she exhibited rapid involuntary eye movements, tremulous hand and finger movements, and an unsteady gait. The gait instability gradually improved, and she regained the ability to walk without falling. Over the next 3 months, she had two episodes of febrile illness with transient increases in gait unsteadiness. At 48 months, she experienced febrile encephalopathy with seizures and was bedridden for 10 days before returning to baseline. She was then started on oral valproic acid. At 54 months, she developed slowly progressive hearing loss. At 60 months, she presented with the ability to walk without support, speak in two-word sentences, dress and undress, and feed herself. There was no history of visual impairment or similar illnesses in her family. Examination at 60 months revealed normal anthropometry, left convergent squint, horizontal nystagmus, bilateral pale optic discs, hypotonia, areflexia, and perioral and appendicular dyskinesia (intermittent spontaneous jerky movements of fingers, toes, limbs, and lips). Cerebellar examination showed gait incoordination (gait ataxia), truncal hypotonia, intentional tremors, positive finger-nose test, dysdiadochokinesia, and incoordinated slurred speech (scanning speech). Pes cavus was not present.
Diagnostic Tests: A targeted sequencing of ATP1A3 gene revealed a pathogenic heterozygous missense variant in exon 18 (c.2491G>A, p.E831K).

Case Information: A 61-year-old male reported experiencing a painful mass in the left epididymis for several months. There was no fever or history of trauma associated with the condition. Hematological parameters and urine indexes were found to be within normal limits. Urine culture showed no bacterial growth. Ultrasonography of the left epididymis identified a mass with mixed echotexture located in the epididymal tail.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathology showed an epididymal mass comprising sheets of histiocytes with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm admixed with neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Many of the histiocytes contained small round to oval targetoid structures that were morphologically consistent with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.

Case Information: A 66-year-old female with a medical history of hypertension and depression reported experiencing progressive generalized weakness, fatigability, mild nonspecific headaches, and confusion over the past 10 months. Her condition notably deteriorated in the week prior to her visit, leading to multiple falls. In the emergency department, she denied experiencing visual changes, seizures or seizure-like activity, any specific pattern to her headaches, nausea, vomiting, or other constitutional symptoms. Her neurological examination revealed no apparent focal neurological deficits and was within normal limits.
Diagnostic Tests: Computed tomography scan of the head showed an intraventricular mass lesion with associated obstructive hydrocephalus. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with gadolinium, time-of-flight angiogram, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy sequences was obtained for further delineation of the lesion and operative planning. The lesion was approximately 2.8 × 4.1 × 3.9 cm in maximal transverse by anterior posterior by craniocaudal dimensions. It was localized to the inferior aspect of the right lateral ventricle, contacting the septum pellucidum, and extending through the right foramen of Monro into the third ventricle. It expanded the ventricle without evidence of parenchymal invasion. It also appeared to come into contact with the inner surface of the body of corpus callosum. The lesion appeared to have a diffuse pattern of enhancement on T1 + Gd sequences. It seemed of intermediate intensity on T2-weighted sequences. It had uniformly low-grade restricted diffusion. There was no calcification or evidence of hemorrhage. MR angiogram showed small branching vessels within and along the margin of the mass. MR spectroscopy showed markedly elevated choline peak and diminished but preserved N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) peak.

Case Information: A 26-year-old Japanese male experienced severe headache and nausea for about 3 weeks. He had a previous episode that involved convulsion-like symptoms. Imaging revealed a cystic nodular lesion approximately 60 mm in diameter in the left parietal lobe of the cerebrum. Medication was given, leading to symptom relief. However, 12 days later, his symptoms worsened, and he was admitted to the emergency department at the University of Miyazaki Hospital.
Diagnostic Tests: MRI showed a mass of 70 × 53 × 57 mm in the left temporoparietal lobe. A solid element with slight hypointensity on T1-weighted and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images along the dura mater was noted. Cystic changes were likely associated with the sanguineous fluid. A peritumoral band with hyperintensity on T2-weighted image was observed at the periphery of the lesion, suggesting an extra-axial lesion. A dural tail sign was also noted on the gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted image. The lesion appeared to be focally infiltrative to the brain surface, but no apparent connection to the ventricle was observed.

Case Information: The patient is a 3-year-and-11-month-old female, the second child of healthy parents with a healthy 10-year-old elder brother. She was delivered via full-term cesarean section with a birth weight of 3300 g and a head circumference larger than the normal range. She exhibited hand deformities, including flexed hands and outward-tilting fingers that could not be extended. At 5 months, she was unable to look up or turn over. Following rehabilitation training, she could walk with support and say simple words like 'Mom' and 'Dad.' Rehabilitation training was discontinued thereafter. By age 3, she could walk and run independently but still only spoke a few simple words. Currently, her height is in the 97th percentile for her age group, and her weight exceeds the 97th percentile for children of the same age. She has experienced regression in language development and is unable to engage in routine communication. Her facial features include a protruding forehead, a head circumference of 57 cm, oblique cleft eyes, widely spaced eyes, a long mandibular tip, and hair thinning in both temporal areas. Except for the thumbs, the other four fingers on both hands are excessively outward, and her palms lack palm prints. The first seizure occurred at 3-and-a-half years old, characterized by cyanotic lips, dyspnea, stiffness, and fever, resolving spontaneously after 2–3 minutes.
Diagnostic Tests: De novo heterozygous variant was found by WES in trios: NSD1 (NM_022455.5), c.6095G > A, p.TRP2032*. EEG showed abnormal discharges in occipital area. MRI displayed that the ventricle was slightly larger.

Case Information: A 37-year-old woman with a history of gestational diabetes was admitted following a motor vehicle accident for evaluation of recurrent low blood sugar levels. She initially experienced a loss of consciousness due to a witnessed seizure, which improved after receiving 5% dextrose (D5W) at the accident scene. She had no memory of the event, and her initial blood glucose level was 32 mg/dL. Neurological, cardiovascular, and respiratory examinations showed no abnormalities. Upon arrival at the emergency department, she was not in status epilepticus, had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12, and exhibited normal vital signs. Her psychomotor activity, perception, and cognitive functions were normal. During her hospital stay, she had recurrent episodes of low blood sugar, both when fasting and after meals, with glucose levels ranging from 32 to 70 mg/dL. Symptoms appeared when glucose levels fell below 50 mg/dL, requiring continuous infusions of 10% dextrose solution. Although she had gestational diabetes three years ago, she had no subsequent diagnosis of diabetes and reported no prior symptoms of low blood sugar such as weakness, sweating, pallor, tremors, confusion, tingling, or visual disturbances in the past year. She also reported no glycopenic symptoms before this hospitalization and was not taking any medications or supplements at home. Tests for insulin autoantibodies and sulfonylurea were negative, and her thyroid function tests were normal. An evaluation for adrenal insufficiency using a cosyntropin stimulation test was also normal.
Diagnostic Tests: A venous glucose measurement of 46 mg/dL yielded noteworthy increases in C-peptide and insulin concentrations. Additionally, there was a notable suppression of beta hydroxybutyrate levels. An abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast revealed a 1.3 cm mass located at the tail of the pancreas.
